events.text: Utterson and Poole search the theatre, cabinet, closets and cellar for Jekyll.
events.quote: All these they now thoroughly examined

events.text: They find the by-street door locked with a rusty broken key lying nearby.
events.quote: It was locked; and lying near by on the flags, they found the key, already stained with rust

events.text: They examine the cabinet and find chemical apparatus and white salt on saucers.
events.quote: there were traces of chemical work, various measured heaps of some white salt being laid on glass saucers

events.text: They find a pious book annotated by Jekyll with startling blasphemies.
events.quote: annotated, in his own hand with startling blasphemies

events.text: They look into the cheval-glass and see only the room and their own pale faces.
events.quote: their own pale and fearful countenances stooping to look in

events.text: Utterson opens an envelope addressed to him and finds a will naming himself instead of Hyde.
events.quote: with indescribable amazement read the name of Gabriel John Utterson

events.text: Utterson reads Jekyll's dated note and concludes Jekyll was alive that day and may have fled.
events.quote: he was alive and here this day

events.text: Poole hands Utterson a sealed packet, the third enclosure.
events.quote: gave into his hands a considerable packet sealed in several places

events.text: Utterson decides to go home, read the documents, and return before midnight to send for the police.
events.quote: I shall be back before midnight, when we shall send for the police

relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls how a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque that proved genuine. Enfield names him Hyde, deformed and detestable, still holding the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

ng, and the red baize door leaped against the lock and hinges. A dismal screech, as of mere animal terror, rang from the cabinet. Up went the axe again, and again the panels crashed and the frame bounded; four times the blow fell; but the wood was tough and the fittings were of excellent workmanship; and it was not until the fifth, that the lock burst and the wreck of the door fell inwards on the carpet.
[P32] The besiegers, appalled by their own riot and the stillness that had succeeded, stood back a little and peered in. There lay the cabinet before their eyes in the quiet lamplight, a good fire glowing and chattering on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin strain, a drawer or two open, papers neatly set forth on the business table, and nearer the fire, the things laid out for tea; the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glazed presses full of chemicals, the most commonplace that night in London.
[P33] Right in the middle there lay the body of a man sorely contorted and still twitching. They drew near on tiptoe, turned it on his back and beheld the face of Edward Hyde. He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes of the doctor’s bigness; the cords of his face still moved with a semblance of life, but life was quite gone; and by the crushed phial in the hand and the strong smell of kernels that hung upon the air, Utterson knew that he was looking on the body of a self-destroyer.
[P34] “We have come too late,” he said sternly, “whether to save or punish. Hyde is gone to his account; and it only remains for us to find the body of your master.”

known_before.name: Mr. Utterson
known_before.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
known_before.bio: G. J. Utterson is a lawyer, a kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and an old friend of both Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past who is troubled by old sins. After Enfield told him of a faceless figure at a by-street door, he lay awake haunted, kept watch by that door, and resolved to hunt for Hyde. known_before.name: Poole
known_before.tagline: Elderly servant at Dr. Jekyll's house
known_before.bio: Poole is the elderly servant at Dr. Jekyll's house, obedient to his master and to Hyde as his superior. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, confirmed Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, said all servants had orders to obey Hyde, and that Hyde never dined there and mostly used the laboratory. He admitted Utterson to Jekyll's cabinet and told him no letter came except by post. He reported that Jekyll had shut his door against Utterson and was confined. Utterson now prefers speaking with Poole

known_before.name: Dr. Jekyll
known_before.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir
known_before.bio: Henry Jekyll is a doctor, connoisseur and old friend of Utterson and Lanyon, known for charities and religion. He is fifty, large, well-made and smooth-faced, with a slyish cast. Over ten years ago Lanyon found him too fanciful and wrong in mind. His will leaves all his possessions to Edward Hyde, who inherits if Jekyll vanishes. When Utterson raised the will and Hyde, Jekyll paled, refused to hear more, called Lanyon a hide-bound pedant, said he could be rid of Hyde whenever he chose, and asked Utterson to help Hy
known_relations: the man in the middle（patron of Hyde）
recent_events: Utterson greets Jekyll and hopes he is better.
Jekyll replies he is very low and says it will not last long.
Utterson introduces his cousin Mr. Enfield to Dr. Jekyll and invites Jekyll out.
Jekyll declines the walk, saying it is quite impossible and he dare not.
Utterson proposes they stay below and talk from where they are.
Jekyll's smile turns to abject terror and the window is thrust down.

known_before.name: the man in the middle
known_before.tagline: Tramples a girl, pays with a cheque
known_before.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He is merciless, inspires enduring hatred, and impresses beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. He later met Utterson at that door, gave his address in Soho, angrily accused Utterson of lying
recent_events: The maid's master had seen Hyde only twice.

Observers agreed only on a sense of unexpressed deformity in Hyde.
Hyde vanishes after Sir Danvers's murder; rewards are offered.

known_before.name: Dr. Lanyon
known_before.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor
known_before.bio: Dr. Lanyon is a doctor with a house in Cavendish Square, an old friend of Utterson and formerly of Dr. Jekyll. He is boisterous, decided and theatrical but genuine. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind. When Utterson asked about Hyde, Lanyon had never heard of him. He dined with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, but later Utterson found him visibly decayed; Lanyon declared himself a doomed man who would never recover, refused to hear Jekyll's name and called him dead to him.
recent_events: Utterson dines with Jekyll and Lanyon as inseparable friends.
Utterson visits Lanyon and is shocked by his decayed appearance.
Lanyon declares himself a doomed man who will never recover.
Lanyon refuses to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him.
Lanyon takes to his bed and dies within a fortnight.
After the funeral Utterson opens Lanyon's sealed envelope.
